title: The Abilene Paradox: Why Your Team Agreed to a Plan Nobody Wanted
author: The Good Boss
summary: The Good Boss uses a personal management failure — a rushed decision to compress a product timeline that three team members privately doubted but never voiced — to introduce Jerry Harvey's Abilene Paradox: a phenomenon where a group commits to a plan nobody individually wants because each member wrongly assumes they're the lone dissenter. The piece walks through Harvey's original 1974 family-road-trip anecdote and breaks the paradox into three near-simultaneous steps: private doubt, a mistaken read of the room, and a rational-seeming choice to stay quiet. Its most useful analytical move is distinguishing the Abilene Paradox from groupthink — groupthink involves real, strong objections suppressed out of fear, while the Abilene Paradox involves mild private hesitation suppressed by a false assumption of consensus, meaning it can strike even teams with strong psychological safety. The practical implication, developed toward a 'Reluctance Check' technique the piece references but doesn't fully unpack in this excerpt, is that leaders need mechanisms that surface private doubt simultaneously across a group rather than relying on someone volunteering dissent.
points: The Abilene Paradox differs from groupthink in kind, not degree: groupthink suppresses a real, articulable objection out of fear, while the Abilene Paradox suppresses a vague, low-confidence doubt because each person wrongly assumes they're the only one who feels it.

Because the paradox doesn't depend on fear or weak psychological safety, the article's sharpest claim is that even high-trust, high-safety teams can still fall into it — meaning 'we have good psychological safety' is not a sufficient defense against bad group decisions.

The three-step mechanism (private doubt, a false read of the room, a rational choice to stay quiet) gives leaders a diagnostic to recognize the pattern in real time, since 'the meeting where everyone nodded but nobody was excited' is a recognizable failure mode.

The author's own anecdote — where three separate 1:1s revealed unspoken doubt about a group decision that looked unanimous in the room — is offered as a template for how leaders discover the paradox only after the fact, underscoring the need to surface doubt before, not after, decisions lock in.
quotes: Over the next few days after that decision, in separate 1:1s, three different people on my team told me that they weren't quite sure about the timeline. All of them were in the meeting, but not one of them had said a word in the room.
And that's how a team of smart, honest people ends up committing to a plan that, individually, none of them wanted. This was an example of the Abilene Paradox in action.
When a group agrees to do something that nobody in the group actually wants, because everyone assumes they're the only one who is not into it.

The most subtle, and dangerous, part of the Abilene Paradox is this: nobody in the room is being dishonest or spineless. Each person is making a reasonable decision based on the wrong assumption about what everyone else believes.
Groupthink is what happens when a group actively suppresses real dissent to protect harmony. Someone in the room has a real, strong objection.

It's closer to "I have a nagging feeling, but everyone else looks fine, so it's probably just me." The fix in this case is making everyone's private hesitation visible to everyone else at the same time, before the group locks in on the wrong direction.
This is what makes the Abilene Paradox dangerous. A team can have excellent psychological safety, yet still run into the trap of the paradox.
